diagnosis_explanation:
Your heart has a problem with its arteries. These arteries supply blood to your heart muscle. Your coronary arteries were narrowed. This is called coronary artery disease. A procedure was done to open these blocked arteries. This procedure is called a percutaneous coronary artery intervention. This helped blood flow to your heart.

You also have a bladder cancer. It was treated with surgery. You had surgery to remove the tumor from your bladder.

You have diabetes. This means your body has trouble using sugar for energy. Your blood sugar needs to be watched.

You have dyslipidemia. This means you have high levels of certain fats in your blood. This can lead to problems.

You have high blood pressure. This is also called hypertension. It means the pressure of blood in your body is too high.

You have a narrowing in a blood vessel in your neck. This vessel is called the carotid artery. It supplies blood to your brain. Surgery was done to fix this. It was called a right carotid endarterectomy. You had this surgery in the past.

You also had your appendix removed a long time ago. You had surgery on your ankle a long time ago too.
medication_rationale:
Plavix:
This medicine helps prevent blood clots.
It is given to keep your treated arteries open.
You might notice bruises more easily.
This is a common effect.
Call your doctor if you have unusual bruising.
Also call if you see blood in your urine or stool.
Call 911 right away if you have sudden face drooping, arm weakness, or trouble speaking.
recovery_trajectory:
**Week 1:**
- You will feel tired after coming home.
- You may have some chest discomfort. This is normal.
- Do not lift anything heavier than 10 pounds.
- Do not drive a car for the first two days.
- Do not soak in a bathtub or pool.
- Eat low-fat, low-salt, and low-cholesterol foods.
- Follow a heart-healthy diabetic diet.
- Call your doctor if you see bleeding or swelling.

**Week 2:**
- Your energy levels should start to slowly return.
- Mild chest discomfort may continue but should lessen.
- Do not immerse your body in water, like baths or pools. Showers are fine.
- Keep following your low-fat, low-salt diet.
- Continue to eat foods that are good for diabetes and your heart.
- Your goal this week is to walk short distances inside your home.
- Watch for signs of infection like redness or fever. Call your doctor if you see them.

**Week 3:**
- You may start to feel more comfortable moving around.
- Continue to avoid heavy lifting or strenuous activities.
- You can do light tasks around your house.
- You can now immerse yourself in water, like baths or hot tubs.
- Keep up with your special diet for your heart and diabetes.
- Your goal this week is to walk for 10 to 15 minutes outside.
- Call your doctor if you notice swelling in your legs or feet.

**Week 4:**
- Most days should feel easier than the week before.
- You can likely do more of your usual daily activities.
- Continue to avoid lifting anything over 10 pounds.
- Keep your diet heart-healthy and good for diabetes.
- Your goal this week is to walk a bit longer each day.
- Call your doctor if you have heavy bleeding or signs of infection.

**When to expect improvement:**
- You should feel a steady increase in energy over the next weeks.
- Continue all your diet plans for long-term heart health.
- Follow up with your doctor as scheduled.
- Healing takes time, so be patient with yourself.
escalation_guide:
CALL 911 IMMEDIATELY
These symptoms are life-threatening. Do not drive yourself.
- Bleeding that will not stop: You are losing too much blood.
- Sudden trouble breathing: Your body needs oxygen right now.
- Chest pain or pressure: Your heart needs help fast.
- Signs of stroke: face drooping, arm weakness, trouble speaking.
- Seizure or fainting spells.

GO TO THE ER TODAY
Do not wait until tomorrow. Go within a few hours.
- Swelling in arms or legs: Fluid may be building up.
- Signs of infection: red streaks, pus, or warm skin.
- Fever over 101 degrees F: You may have an infection.

CALL YOUR DOCTOR
Call during office hours. Do not go to the ER for these.
- Bleeding that is not bad: Use pressure to slow it.
- Mild swelling without pain: This can happen while you heal.
- Questions about your Plavix: Your nurse can help you plan.
